opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first attempt was humbling. Going in, the assumption, and I think a lot of people shared it, was that if you just put images and text into one sequence, train a single model on enough interleaved web data, and let next-token prediction do its work, then understanding and generation would naturally reinforce each other. That's the story we'd learned from language models: scale plus a unified objective gives you emergence.

What we actually saw was more complicated. The model got reasonably good at understanding, and it could generate images that were okay, but the two abilities didn't really help each other the way we hoped. In some cases they even seemed to compete. Pushing generation quality up could hurt understanding, and vice versa. So the first lesson was that "unified architecture" is not the same as "unified capability." You can put everything in one network and still end up with two skills living side by side rather than one integrated intelligence.

The second lesson was about the data. Interleaved web data looks rich, but if you look closely, the images and text are often only loosely related. A picture next to a paragraph doesn't mean the text describes the picture, or that the picture follows from the text. In language, the next token is strongly constrained by context. In interleaved data, the next image is often barely constrained at all. So the model can't learn much causal or reasoning structure from it. It learns correlation, style, maybe some layout, but not the kind of deep dependency that would force understanding and generation to share the same internal representation.

And the third lesson, which I think is the most important, is about representation. Images are very high-dimensional, and a lot of that information is perceptual detail that matters for generation but is almost irrelevant for understanding. Text, by contrast, is already highly compressed and semantic. When you force both into the same token space, you face a real tension: do the visual tokens capture semantics or pixels? Tokenizers optimized for reconstruction are not great for understanding, and tokenizers optimized for semantics give you poor generation. That trade-off didn't go away just because we scaled up.

So my understanding shifted from "unification is mainly an engineering and scale problem" to "unification is a problem about what objective, what data, and what representation would actually make generation require understanding." In language, generation and understanding are the same thing because predicting the next word well requires understanding. For vision, we haven't yet found the equivalent setting where generating the next image truly requires reasoning. I think until we find that, whether through better data like video, or through tasks where the image is genuinely the consequence of thinking, the unified model will remain somewhat of a marriage of convenience rather than a true synergy.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that first attempt was humbling. Going in, I had the fairly naive assumption that if you just concatenate images and text into one sequence, use a single next-token objective, and scale it up, the model would naturally learn to both understand and generate. The elegance of the idea was almost seductive. Language modeling had worked that way, so why wouldn't multimodal?

What we found was that the two tasks pull the representation in different directions. Understanding wants the image tokens to be semantic, compressed, aligned with language concepts. Generation wants them to preserve pixel-level detail, texture, layout, things that a good caption would never mention. When you force one tokenizer and one objective to serve both, you end up with a model that is mediocre at each. The generation side in particular suffered badly. The samples looked plausible from a distance but fell apart on fine structure, and the understanding side was weaker than a dedicated vision-language model trained with a fraction of the compute.

The deeper realization was that the bottleneck was not the architecture or the loss function. It was the data. Interleaved web data is mostly weakly aligned. The image and the surrounding text are related, but the text rarely explains the image in a way that would let the model learn a tight bidirectional mapping. So the model learned a lot of loose correlations and very little of the precise conditional structure you need for controllable generation. That pushed us to think much harder about data construction, about what kind of image-text pairs actually teach generation versus what merely teaches recognition.

The other thing it changed for me was how I think about the visual representation itself. I came away convinced that the choice of visual tokenizer is where most of the real difficulty hides. If the representation is wrong, no amount of scaling the language backbone will rescue it. So in later work we spent far more effort on the encoder and decoder side, on whether the representation should be discrete or continuous, and on how much semantic prior to bake in versus how much reconstruction fidelity to keep.

So the short version is that the first attempt taught me that unification is not free. You do not get it by gluing modalities together. You get it by carefully deciding what the shared representation should carry, and by building data that actually forces the model to use it in both directions.

astra-6.text:
That first attempt made me realize that putting images and text into the same sequence is only the starting point. You can give the model a unified format and a single training objective, but that doesn’t automatically mean generation and understanding will reinforce each other.

Understanding often requires the model to focus on the meaning of an image and ignore irrelevant detail. Generation requires it to preserve enough detail to actually produce an image. So the challenge becomes: what representation can support both, and how do you balance the training so one capability doesn’t dominate the other?

Interleaving also makes the relationship between images and text important. The model needs to learn why an image appears at a particular point, what the surrounding text says about it, and how that image changes what comes next. Simply mixing image and text data doesn’t guarantee that.

So my understanding shifted from thinking of unification primarily as an architecture problem to thinking about the whole training system—the representation, the data, and the objective together. A shared sequence gives you a framework; learning useful connections between the modalities is the real work.

sol-6.1.text:
I initially thought the main challenge was finding a common representation for images and text. If we could put them into one sequence and train a model to predict what comes next, perhaps generation and understanding would emerge together.

That first attempt made me realize that sharing a sequence format is only the starting point. The important question is what the training actually forces the model to learn. It can predict text while using very little visual information, or generate an image without developing the kind of detailed understanding you need for answering questions about it.

So I started thinking much more about the relationship between the data, the representation, and the objective. Does the interleaving require the model to connect a particular sentence to a particular image? Does the visual representation preserve the details needed for understanding while still being useful for generation? And are the different training signals helping each other?

For me, the lesson was that a unified model needs more than a unified architecture. You have to create conditions where understanding helps generation, and generation encourages better understanding. Putting both tasks into the same model doesn’t automatically give you that.
